output.summary: Atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response is an established cause of arrhythmic cardiac syncope, particularly during episodes of 1:1 AV conduction. ESC 2018 and ACC/AHA/HRS 2017 guidelines support ECG documentation and cardiac monitoring as the primary diagnostic tools. Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is the preferred definitive therapy for typical atrial flutter. Anticoagulation is guided by CHA2DS2-VASc scoring, with identical risk stratification to atrial fibrillation.

alternatives: Diltiazem (non-DHP CCB): alternative rate-control agent when beta-blocker is contraindicated; do not combine with beta-blocker.
Rivaroxaban or dabigatran: alternative direct oral anticoagulants if apixaban is not tolerated.
contraindications: Concurrent use of a beta-blocker and a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (verapamil, diltiazem) for rate control: risk of symptomatic bradycardia, high-degree AV block, and hemodynamic compromise — avoid combination without specialist oversight.
Digoxin combined with additional AV-nodal agents: additive risk of bradycardia and high-degree AV block during flutter; monitor closely if combination used.
NSAIDs or aspirin combined with apixaban without a compelling indication: additive bleeding risk.
interactions: Metoprolol + Hydrochlorothiazide: additive antihypertensive effect; monitor blood pressure and heart rate during titration.
Apixaban + Atorvastatin: no clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction at standard doses; both are CYP3A4/P-gp substrates but combination is generally well tolerated at standard dosing.

warnings: If cardioversion is planned: anticoagulation must be therapeutic for at least 3 weeks prior, or transesophageal echocardiogram must be performed to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus, per standard AF/flutter cardioversion protocols.
Monitor potassium and renal function periodically with concurrent HCTZ and lisinopril — electrolyte disturbances can affect atrial conduction.
Lisinopril: monitor for hypotension if additional antihypertensive or rate-control agents are added.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Robert Caldwell is a 67-year-old Caucasian male with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes (diet-controlled), and hyperlipidemia who presents to the emergency department by ambulance after a single episode of transient loss of consciousness. His neighbor, who had stopped by for a visit, reports that the patient was standing at his kitchen counter when he suddenly collapsed without any prodromal warning, falling forward and catching himself partially on the countertop. He was unresponsive for an estimated 10 to 15 seconds, then regained consciousness spontaneously and immediately asked what had happened. There was no convulsive activity, no tonic stiffening, no rhythmic jerking, no tongue biting, and no urinary incontinence. Recovery was described as immediate and complete — he was coherent and conversational within 30 seconds. The neighbor noted that just before the event the patient had commented he felt his heart 'racing' for a few seconds. He endorses approximately three months of episodic palpitations that he describes as a rapid fluttering sensation in his chest, generally lasting 10 to 30 minutes and resolving on their own. His primary care physician evaluated him for these episodes eight weeks ago. An ECG performed in the office at that visit showed a rate of 88 bpm with a regular rhythm and was documented as 'sinus rhythm, normal.' He was reassured that the palpitations were likely related to anxiety given an ongoing stressful period following retirement, and no further workup was arranged at that time. He has not been started on any new medications. He denies chest pain, dyspnea at rest, exertional pre-syncope, fever, recent illness, or ingestion of stimulants or new supplements. He has had no prior syncopal episodes. On review of systems, he endorses fatigue for the past two to three months and mild exertional dyspnea when climbing stairs, which he attributed to deconditioning.
